The vulns are with GoAhead Web Server which is a backend library used by these devices. There's a patch available from GoAhead but that doesn't mean there's a patch available for the devices yet -- that's up to the manufacturer.

- TLS traffic over DHE ciphers have a 1-byte secret, "04", meaning anyone can decrypt connections to these devices and steal login credentials and session tokens if the client negotiated with DHE ciphers like the latest TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256, which is extremely likely.

- OpenSSL Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) are not enforced, meaning if a user device is stolen or compromised, and you revoke that mTLS cert, nothing actually happens. There are a lot of other attacks this can be used for.

These are critical because these types of devices run our world. Water systems, electricity, military, firewalls, critical infrastructure.

items.content:
Growing up with financial struggles, in a village or town, with mostly regional-language education shaped my confidence. My school called itself English medium, but hardly anyone taught in English.

My parents worked hard to support me. But I was also taught not to question them or any elder, teacher, police officer, rich person, or city person. I grew up feeling like I should always obey and never speak up.

That followed me into engineering and work. Struggling to express myself, stumbling over words during presentations, sweating, finding it hard to say no. Being the obedient “nice guy” comes at a cost.

Many people around the world grow up this way, constantly worrying about how others see them, afraid of humiliation or awkwardness, and holding themselves back from taking risks.

I’m learning to push myself out of my comfort zone, speak up, and stand up for myself. It’s okay to express your thoughts and clarify what you mean when someone misunderstands you. You don’t have to silently accept their version of you.

Let yourself be awkward while you practise. Trust me, people care far less about your awkward moments than you think. They have their own lives and worries.

That’s how you grow and build confidence. With practice, you can communicate more clearly, feel more comfortable during presentations, and perform better at work. You don’t have to keep holding yourself back.

Ask questions. Say no. Make mistakes. Express yourself. Just be mindful of your words and be kind.

We love grep, but there's more to security code review than searching for dangerous functions and patterns.

Those searches can give you useful starting points, but the real work is understanding what the application does, how its security controls work, and where its assumptions break down.

A missing authorisation check won't necessarily contain a suspicious keyword, and a business logic flaw might use perfectly safe functions in the wrong order.

Use grep to find places to look, but always take the time to understand what you're reviewing..

items.content:
The first thing that looked strange was not on the user’s laptop.

It was on the file server.

A workstation called WS-214 suddenly authenticated to our Finance share using an account called:

svc-reporting

That account was supposed to belong to an old reporting service.

It had no reason to be coming from a normal employee workstation.

So I checked the Security logs on the file server.

Event ID 4624 showed a successful network logon.

Logon Type: 3

The account was CORP\svc-reporting, and the source was WS-214.

A few seconds later, Event ID 5140 showed the same account accessing:

\\FS-08\Finance

Now I wanted to know what happened on the workstation before that connection.

The process logs showed PowerShell launching cmd.exe, and the command line included a net use connection to the Finance share using the service account.

That was enough to treat it as possible lateral movement.

I checked the account in Active Directory.

Its description still said:

Legacy reporting service

The password had not been changed since February 2025.

That told us something else.

This was an old service credential that had been sitting around for a long time.

We isolated WS-214, disabled the account, rotated the credentials and started checking every system that had used svc-reporting.

We also reviewed the Finance share to see what had been accessed during the session.

What stood out to me was that the attacker did not need some complicated exploit to move between systems.

They had a valid credential.

Windows accepted it.

SMB accepted it.

From the network’s point of view, the login looked legitimate.

That is why stale service accounts can be dangerous.

They normally run quietly for years, people forget who owns them, password rotation gets skipped, and eventually nobody is really watching where they are being used from.

Sometimes lateral movement does not look like an exploit.

It looks like a successful login from the wrong machine.

items.content:
RT @merill: Folks,

I left Microsoft three months ago to start my own company. Two weeks after I left, my whole team in Australia was let go.

I see the hurt it’s causing my ex-colleagues, their families and their kids. Layoffs, forced relocations, PIPs. It’s brutal and I don’t want to brush past that.

But here’s my honest take.

Microsoft needs fewer people.

I’ve been on the inside. I’ve seen how things get built. Lots of small orgs. Layers on layers. Silos everywhere.

Here’s a real example.

The Entra team shipped managed identities back in 2017. No more secrets in code. A clear security win.

Then they tried to get the rest of Microsoft to adopt it. Very few teams did, and the ones that did moved at a snail’s pace. Every org had its own priorities and its own decision makers.

It took Microsoft getting hacked, and the Secure Future Initiative that followed, before things really moved.

Today almost every Microsoft app and service supports managed identity.

Six years, and a major breach, to get there.

In a world with agents and fewer people, that rollout would be possible across Microsoft in months, not years.

Microsoft already has everything else. The customers. The infrastructure. The scale.

What it needs is fewer people, leaning hard into agentic work.

Right now OpenAI and Anthropic are shipping at a pace Microsoft can’t match.

Microsoft has to change to survive.

The vulns are with GoAhead Web Server which is a backend library used by these devices. There's a patch available from GoAhead but that doesn't mean there's a patch available for the devices yet -- that's up to the manufacturer.

- TLS traffic over DHE ciphers have a 1-byte secret, "04", meaning anyone can decrypt connections to these devices and steal login credentials and session tokens if the client negotiated with DHE ciphers like the latest TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256, which is extremely likely.

- LibreSSL mTLS has been completely bypassed, meaning anyone can connect over mTLS. If you have one of these devices listening on the internet and are expecting mTLS to protect it from attackers, take it offline or patch asap.

- OpenSSL Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) are not enforced, meaning if a user device is stolen or compromised, and you revoke that mTLS cert, nothing actually happens. There are a lot of other attacks this can be used for.

These are critical because these types of devices run our world. Water systems, electricity, military, firewalls, critical infrastructure.

items.content:
This is an impressive amount of FUD built around an AI agent that was given a detection engineering task.

Cohere asked the model to write a detection rule for curl-based malware delivery. Anyone with practical experience in detection engineering knows that writing a rule is only part of the job.

You examine the environment, generate or collect relevant telemetry, inspect the resulting events, write the rule, test it and refine it. You don’t just guess what the logs might look like.

Even Microsoft’s CTI-REALM benchmark, which Cohere used here, explicitly involves tool use, telemetry exploration and iterative rule validation.

So why exactly is an agent using tools and executing commands so unexpected?

Was this particular PUT request part of such a workflow? We don’t know. Cohere doesn’t establish that. But the published command sends a hardcoded test string, not a diagnostic file containing sensitive information. And Cohere admits it hasn’t established the root cause.

Yet somehow this turns into an article about potentially backdoored Chinese AI models, secret callbacks, national security risks and the dangers of open-weight models, followed by a pitch for Cohere’s own products.

From a technical perspective, the conclusions are wildly disproportionate to the evidence presented.

I can only see two explanations: Either nobody with practical detection engineering experience reviewed this before publication, or the framing was a deliberate attempt to influence public opinion about Chinese open-weight models.

Neither is a particularly good look for a company presenting this as security research.
